newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New EU plans to cut car pollution face rocky road.
newsitem.headline: New EU plans to cut car pollution face rocky road.

text.p: European Union environment ministers could fail to resolve their differences next month over draft EU rules on vehicle engine emissions and fuel quality, designed to cut air pollution by 2010.

The EU states are deeply divided over European Commission proposals to introduce in 2000 stricter limits on the level of sulphur, benzene and other pollutants in motor fuels, senior Commission energy official Johannes Maters said on Wednesday.

Governments are also split over the precise timing of a ban on leaded petrol, which the Commission wants to bring in by 2000, and disagree over the need to set even stricter emission reduction targets for 2005, Maters told a conference on refining, vehicle technology and fuel quality.

Southern countries like Spain and Portugal, whose refineries import highly sulphurous crude oil from the Gulf, would have great difficulty meeting the Commission's target of cutting the maximum sulphur content in diesel from 500 to 350 parts per million (ppm) in 2000, another EU official told Reuters.
Refining industries could move operations out of the EU altogether if the 15-member bloc imposed too strict fuel quality requirements, the official, who declined to be identified, said.
By contrast, several northern EU states were pressing for even tighter limits on pollutants, Maters said.
He predicted the Dutch, who hold the EU presidency, would have difficulty achieving their goal of brokering a compromise at the June 19-20 environment ministers meeting in Brussels.
Even if a provisional deal is reached in June, there will be arduous negotiations with the European Parliament before the draft rules become law, Maters said.

On April 10 the EU assembly adopted dozens of amendments to tighten the Commission's draft fuel and engine standards, including cutting the benzene level in petrol from two to one percent and the sulphur content from 200 to 30 ppm.

Maters, himself a Dutchman and a former employee of the Anglo-Dutch oil company Shell, said he did not agree with the parliament's demands, arguing that the Commission had worked closely with the oil and car industries to produce limits that were cost-effective and took into account the strategic economic and job-providing importance of these sectors.
Mats Fredriksson, oil giant Texaco's strategy adviser, told the conference parliament's changes would produce "minor improvements, while the cost escalates five- or six-fold".
But the assembly has the backing of Arco Chemical, which pioneers "cleaner" reformulated motor fuels.
Arco's director of government relations in Europe Jonathan Kapstein told Reuters the limits proposed by the parliament were "very strict but...perfectly achievable on the fuel side".

Parliament's demands on sulphur and benzene limits -- which both produce air-borne pollutants that damage human health -- are also mirrored in the Fuel Charter agreed by the European car manufacturers association (ACEA) in 1994.
The Commission will in 1999 consider putting forward even tougher fuel and engine standards for 2005 but it may find it more difficult to get industry support this time.

Texaco's Fredriksson said Europe's problems could be solved by the Commission's current proposals and insisted any future attempts to improve air quality should target pollution from sources other than the transport sector, such as power stations.
